# The finished model with everything the book has not introduced by the end
# of ch02 removed, so that a reader can see it at 8 nodes. Not a model
# anybody would ship. Do not edit: say which chapter introduces a node in
# build-order.yaml instead.
model: web_service_demand
title: >-
  A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts — What
  arrives, and what accumulates
currency: USD
description: The web service model as it stands at the end of ch02.
nodes:
  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    value: 8000
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        This figure comes from the forecaster, who holds a spread
        of plausible busy-hour rates and rounds it to one. ch04
        replaces the one number with the spread.
    range: [500, 40000]
  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how
      much you hold today. Nobody can count next quarter's busy
      hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they
      grow, and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the
      level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        stated workload (ch02) — what the service holds today:
        its database and the objects users have uploaded, before
        replication, indexes or compression
    range: [1, 200]
  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    value: 1.3
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        Chosen, not measured. One number cannot say how sure you
        are of it, so ch04 replaces it with a spread.
    range: [1.0, 2.0]
  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: the refresh cycle this fleet is bought against
    range: [3, 8]
  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n
      the n is a pure number, so the horizon has to be divided
      by something with the same units before it can be used as
      one. Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year
  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
outputs: [peak_request_rate, stored_data]
correlations: []

files.model.yaml:
model: web_service
title: A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts
currency: USD

description: >-
  The book's running example: a service that takes requests and keeps records, run on some
  number of ordinary hosts, sized from a stated workload and costed over five years. Requests
  arrive and data accumulates; a host has cores, memory and disk, and each of those is a chain
  that ends in a count of hosts. One of the three binds.

  It is a conditional model. Its ceilings are the queueing knee, the point where more hosts stop
  helping, the working set outgrowing memory, disk filling, and a host dying at the busy hour;
  its one measured constant is how well the stored records compress. Its one rate constant —
  CPU time per request — belongs on a rig nobody has declared, and is held as a labelled claim
  until one is.

  Vendor-neutral by construction. Nothing below names a product; every figure is a workload
  assumption, a price you would get quoted, a spec sheet, or the measured constant.

nodes:

  # -- the workload: what arrives, and what accumulates -----------------------------------------

  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3000.0, likely: 8000.0, maximum: 20000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — the busy hour, not the daily mean. Triangular because this is an engineer's
        min/likely/max and pretending to more shape than that would be invention."
    range: [500, 40000]

  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how much you hold today. Nobody can
      count next quarter's busy hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they grow,
      and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "stated workload (ch02) — what the service holds today: its database and the
        objects users have uploaded, before replication, indexes or compression"
    range: [1, 200]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.12, p90: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and cannot be negative. The p10/p90
        say: surprised below 12% a year, surprised above 60%. One factor for requests and for
        records, because users drive both."
    range: [1.0, 2.0]

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the refresh cycle this fleet is bought against"
    range: [3, 8]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n the n is a pure number, so the
      horizon has to be divided by something with the same units before it can be used as one.
      Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  # -- the host: the first numbers somebody else supplied --------------------------------------

  cores_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core/host
    value: 16
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: physical cores. A hyperthread is not a core, and a sheet that counts
        threads doubles this number without doubling the work a host does (ch07)"
    range: [4, 128]

  ram_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 64
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: the modules fitted. The sheet says 64 GB and means GiB — appendix D —
        and the operating system will report less than either, which is os_reserve's job"
    range: [8, 1024]

  os_reserve:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.06, likely: 0.10, maximum: 0.18}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the share of memory the kernel, the agents and the page cache floor keep before
        the service sees any. Triangular: a floor, a usual figure, and a host with too many
        agents on it"
    range: [0.0, 0.4]

  ram_for_service:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per host
    note: >-
      Gibibytes in, decimal terabytes out — the build converts (appendix D). Declared in the
      unit the working set is counted in, so that the chain which divides one by the other
      rounds a count of hosts and not a count of hosts times nine hundred and thirty-one.
    formula: ram_per_host * (1 - os_reserve)

  # -- peak and mean --------------------------------------------------------------------------

  peak_to_mean:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: peak-to-mean ratio
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 3.5, maximum: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — the busy hour against the daily mean. Triangular, and it is a property of
        your traffic that belongs to the estate target: nothing here can measure it"
    range: [1.0, 10.0]

  mean_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: mean request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate / peak_to_mean

  # -- Little's law: how busy the fleet is -----------------------------------------------------

  service_demand:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: second * core / request
    label: CPU time per request
    note: >-
      Core-seconds of work one request costs, which is not how long a request takes. A request
      that occupies one core for twelve milliseconds has a service demand of twelve milliseconds
      whether it returns in twelve milliseconds or in twelve seconds — the difference is
      queueing, and Part II is about that difference.

      This is the model's one rate constant and it belongs on a rig (ch03). No rig is declared,
      so it is held here as an assumption whose source says what would replace it, rather than
      as a measured node with nothing behind it.
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.008, likely: 0.012, maximum: 0.020}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "held as an assumption because no reference machine is declared in rig/machine.yml;
        `make measure-rig` on a declared machine replaces this node with a measured one.
        Triangular *because* it has not been measured: once it is, the shape becomes a normal
        around the measurement, which is a change of claim and not only of numbers (ch13)"
    range: [0.002, 0.05]

  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: host
    value: 54
    label: hosts in the fleet
    note: >-
      **The most important node in this model, and the one a spreadsheet hides.** Sizing does not
      produce a fleet; it produces a recommendation, and then a person decides. It arrives here,
      in Part II, because a queue needs something to stand in front of — but it is decided in
      ch12, and everything downstream of it, every dollar, every watt, every ceiling, is a
      consequence of the number chosen here and not of the number the model would recommend in
      hindsight.

      Deriving it instead would make the ceilings below tautologies: a fleet sized to sit under
      the knee sits under it in every future, and the model would cheerfully report a zero per
      cent chance of queueing. Making it an input is what lets the ceilings ask the only question
      worth asking — *given what we actually bought, how often does the world break it?*
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the sizing decision, taken the way it is usually taken: hosts_recommended
        evaluated at every input's point estimate. Change this number and watch the ceilings
        move — that is the exercise of ch12"
    range: [4, 200]

  one_host:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: host
    value: 1
    note: "as elsewhere: a conversion has to be a host before the division means anything"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  one_core:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: core
    value: 1
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  one_request:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: request
    value: 1
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores in the fleet
    formula: hosts * cores_per_host

  busy_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores busy at the busy hour
    note: >-
      Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of cores doing work, it has nothing to do
      with how many you own, and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_demand

  utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: busy_cores / cores

  service_seconds:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: service time
    note: "service demand with the core divided out: how long one request would take alone"
    formula: service_demand * one_request / one_core

  in_flight_unqueued:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in flight, if none waited
    note: >-
      Little's law with the residence time equal to the service time: the fewest requests that
      can be in the system at this arrival rate. ch06 replaces the service time with what a
      request actually waits, and this number goes up.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_seconds

  # -- the knee ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  utilisation_cap:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation the model will admit to
    note: >-
      A modelling choice, stated rather than hidden. The waiting-time formula below divides by
      what is left of the fleet, so at a utilisation of one it divides by zero and returns
      infinity. Infinity is not a prediction. Past this point the formula has stopped describing a
      queue and started describing an arithmetic accident, so the model clamps and the ceiling
      reports that it is over.
    value: 0.98
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "where this model stops being about queues (ch06)"}

  queueing_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.3
    label: queueing margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch06 — how far under the knee the fleet is sized to run at the busy hour. Declared
        once, here, and used by the sizing chain and by the ceiling that checks it, so the two
        cannot drift apart"
    range: [0.0, 0.6]

  effective_utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: min(utilisation, utilisation_cap)

  residence_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: residence time
    note: >-
      Service time divided by the fraction of the fleet that is idle. That single division is
      ch06's whole subject: it is nearly flat while there is slack and nearly vertical when there
      is not, and nothing about the arithmetic warns you which side you are on.
    formula: service_seconds / (1 - effective_utilisation)

  waiting_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: time spent queueing
    formula: residence_time - service_seconds

  concurrency:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in the system
    note: >-
      Little's law, and the only relationship in Part II that is always true: the number of
      requests in a system is the rate they arrive at times how long each one stays. No
      pattern of arrivals assumed, no queue discipline assumed, nothing assumed except that the system
      is in a steady state. ch05 is about what that buys and what it does not.
    formula: peak_request_rate * residence_time

  queueing_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation at the busy hour
    of: utilisation
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      Not a capacity limit: a fleet at ninety per cent has not run out of anything, it has a
      queue in front of it. The margin is large because the cost of crossing it is paid in
      latency by every request, not in a failure somebody gets paged for (ch06).

  # -- what more hosts buy ----------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_count:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: hosts / one_host

  single_host_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second/host
    label: throughput of one host alone
    note: >-
      Every core of a host busy on requests and nothing else: the cores divided by the CPU time
      each request costs. The straight line of ch07 is this times the host count, and it is the
      line nobody has ever measured.
    formula: cores_per_host / service_demand

  contention:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: contention
    note: >-
      The fraction of the work that cannot be done in parallel: a lock, a single writer, a shared
      queue. It costs a fixed share of every host you add, so it flattens the scaling curve and
      never bends it downwards.
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.002, likely: 0.005, maximum: 0.015}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch07 — fitted from two measurements, where two exist. Triangular because a fit
        gives a central value and a range rather than a shape, and its maximum is the claim to
        distrust: a serial fraction can always be worse than the one you measured"

  crosstalk:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: crosstalk
    note: >-
      The cost of hosts having to agree with each other, which grows with the number of pairs
      rather than the number of hosts. This is the term that makes the curve turn over: past some
      count, the next host costs more in agreement than it brings in work.
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.5e-5, p90: 9.0e-5}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch07 — fitted, and the harder of the two to fit. Lognormal because it spans an
        order of magnitude and cannot be negative, and because a shape should not assert a hard
        upper bound on a quantity this weakly fitted"

  linear_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: throughput if scaling were free
    formula: hosts * single_host_throughput

  achievable_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: throughput the fleet can actually reach
    note: >-
      The universal scalability law. One host's throughput times the count, divided by what
      contention and crosstalk take back. With crosstalk at zero it is Amdahl's ceiling; with both
      at zero it is the straight line above.
    formula: linear_throughput / (1 + contention * (host_count - 1) + crosstalk * host_count * (host_count - 1))

  scaling_efficiency:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: achievable_throughput / linear_throughput

  scaling_loss:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the fleet doing nothing useful
    of: 1 - scaling_efficiency
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.5
    because: >-
      At half, one host in two is paying for the other's coordination. There is no failure and
      nothing gets paged; the fleet simply costs twice what its work is worth, and it will go on
      doing so until somebody looks. A budget is the only thing this ceiling protects, which is
      why the margin is the loosest in the book and why it is still worth declaring (ch07).

  peak_hosts:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: where adding hosts stops helping
    note: >-
      Where the scalability curve turns over, from the two coefficients alone: the square root of
      one-minus-contention over crosstalk. Past it, throughput falls. It is a property of the
      software, not of the budget, and no amount of money moves it.
    formula: one_host * sqrt((1 - contention) / crosstalk)

  headroom_to_peak:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the peak already built
    formula: host_count / (peak_hosts / one_host)

  utilisation_including_coordination:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    note: >-
      The same fleet's utilisation, worked out from what it can actually deliver rather than from
      what one host could deliver alone. It is higher than the row above, always, and the gap is
      the work the hosts are doing on each other's behalf.
    formula: peak_request_rate / achievable_throughput

  optimism:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: how much the queueing view understated it
    formula: utilisation_including_coordination / utilisation

  coordination_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    of: utilisation_including_coordination
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      The same queueing margin as above, applied to the capacity the fleet actually has rather
      than to the capacity its parts would have had alone. Where the two ceilings disagree, this
      is the one that is about the system you own (ch07).

  # -- the working set: a regime change --------------------------------------------------------

  hot_fraction:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of records touched in a busy hour
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.01, likely: 0.03, maximum: 0.08}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — the working set as a share of everything held. Triangular; nobody measures
        this and everybody has an opinion, and the maximum is a service whose users all look at
        the same week's data"
    range: [0.005, 0.3]

  working_set:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: working set at horizon
    formula: stored_data * hot_fraction

  cache_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: cache margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — how much of the fleet's memory is kept free of the working set, for its
        own daily swing and for the process heaps. Declared once and used by the chain and by
        the ceiling"
    range: [0.0, 0.6]

  fleet_ram:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: memory the service can use, whole fleet
    formula: hosts * ram_for_service

  cache_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: working set against memory
    of: working_set / fleet_ram
    limit: 1
    headroom: cache_margin
    because: >-
      Past the limit, reads that were served from memory go to disk, and the service time per
      request is no longer the number this model was built on: it is a different number, from a
      different regime, and nothing in a chain of multiplications predicts the step (ch08). The
      margin is the working set's own daily swing.

  # -- capacity: from what you hold to what you must buy ---------------------------------------

  record_compression:
    kind: measured
    unit: dimensionless
    label: record compression ratio
    result: records-compression

  replication_factor:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 3
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "three copies of every record, so that a host can die and take its disks with it.
        A different durability scheme substitutes its own factor here and the rest of the model
        is unchanged, which is the point of it being a node"
    range: [1, 4]

  index_overhead:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.30, maximum: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "indexes, the write-ahead log and journals as a multiplier on stored bytes.
        Triangular, and the bounds are for a service with a few indexes per table — a
        search-heavy one is off the top of this range"

  raw_per_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: raw bytes per stored byte
    formula: replication_factor * index_overhead / record_compression

  raw_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: raw disk needed at horizon
    formula: stored_data * raw_per_stored

  disk_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/host
    value: 2
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: one local drive. Decimal TB, not TiB — appendix D, and it is a 10%
        difference"
    range: [1, 60]

  disk_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: disk margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch11 — room to re-replicate a dead host's records onto the survivors, plus what a
        filesystem needs to keep allocating well. Declared once and used by the chain and by the
        ceiling"
    range: [0.0, 0.45]

  hosts_for_storage:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(raw_data / (disk_per_host * (1 - disk_margin)))

  installed_disk:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: hosts * disk_per_host

  disk_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: disk fill at horizon
    of: raw_data / installed_disk
    limit: 1
    headroom: disk_margin
    because: >-
      A fleet whose disks are full cannot take a dead host's records, and a filesystem at 97% is
      a different filesystem. The margin is the same node the sizing used, so the two cannot
      drift apart (ch11). Over the limit means out of space; inside the margin means the
      re-replication reserve has been spent on data.

  # -- three chains, and the one that binds ----------------------------------------------------

  hosts_for_requests:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(busy_cores / (cores_per_host * (1 - queueing_margin)))

  hosts_for_memory:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(working_set / (ram_for_service * (1 - cache_margin)))

  hosts_recommended:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts the model recommends
    note: >-
      Where a reader meets a binding constraint. Three chains produce three host counts and you
      buy the largest, which means that across this model's uncertainty the answer is sometimes
      set by CPU, sometimes by memory and sometimes by disk — and an average of the three is a
      fleet that satisfies none of them.
    formula: max(hosts_for_requests, hosts_for_memory, hosts_for_storage)

  # -- a host dies at the busy hour ------------------------------------------------------------

  hosts_after_failure:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts left when one dies
    formula: hosts - one_host

  utilisation_after_failure:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation with one host down
    formula: busy_cores / (hosts_after_failure * cores_per_host)

  failure_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation with one host down
    of: utilisation_after_failure
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      One host down at the busy hour: its share of the requests lands on the survivors, and the
      question is whether they are still under the knee. N+1 is this ceiling with the margin at
      zero. The margin here is the queueing margin, because a fleet that has lost a host is
      still a queue (ch11).

  # -- capital ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 4500, p90: 9500}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "chassis, CPU, memory, drives and boot media, as configured. Lognormal like any
        price, and wide because a host is a configuration rather than a commodity"

  host_capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: hosts * host_price

  network_price_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 600, likely: 1100, maximum: 2200}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "switch ports, optics and cabling, amortised per host. Triangular rather than
        lognormal, although it is a price: it is a bill of materials divided by a host count
        somebody chose, so the bounds are the plausible designs rather than a market"

  network_capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: hosts * network_price_per_host

  capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: host_capex + network_capex

  # -- running it -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_power:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: W/host
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 220, likely: 300, maximum: 420}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "typical draw under load, per host as configured. Triangular, and one of the few
        inputs here whose bounds are physical rather than editorial: a host cannot draw less
        than it idles at, or more than its supply will give it"

  pue:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: PUE
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.35, maximum: 1.75}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch16 — facility overhead. A multiplier on IT load, and the single number a
        colocation contract is most likely to disagree with you about. Triangular: the minimum
        is a good building, the maximum is a poor one, and below one is impossible"
    range: [1.0, 2.2]

  facility_power:
    kind: derived
    unit: kW
    note: "watts in, kilowatts out — the build converts, nobody divides by a thousand by hand"
    formula: hosts * host_power * pue

  hours_per_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: hour/year
    value: 8766
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: "by definition, 365.25 x 24. The quarter-day is worth about a fifth of a per cent
        over five years — less than this model's other errors, and free to get right"

  annual_energy:
    kind: derived
    unit: kWh/year
    formula: facility_power * hours_per_year

  electricity_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/kWh
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 0.085, p90: 0.21}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "all-in delivered rate including transmission. Lognormal: it cannot go negative and
        its history is multiplicative"
    range: [0.04, 0.45]

  annual_energy_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: annual_energy * electricity_price

  licence_per_core:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/core/year
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 40, p90: 160}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the platform software's per-core licence, as quoted. Lognormal: a price, and a
        wide one, because it is the line item most often negotiated. It is what makes the core
        count a cost as well as a capacity (ch17)"

  licence_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host/year
    value: 0
    label: licence per host
    note: >-
      A declared zero, not an absent line. This quote licenses the platform software per core,
      so its per-host charge is nil and the model says so, with a source. A comparison needs
      the same lines on both sides: a line that one quote does not have is a cost that quote
      never pays, and the only honest way to leave it out is to put it in at zero (ch22).
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the price list: per core, with no per-host charge. A quote that licenses per host
        instead puts its figure here and zero in licence_per_core, and the two totals are then
        compared like for like"
    range: [0, 12000]

  annual_licences:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    note: >-
      Both licence lines, whichever of them a quote uses. One of the two is a declared zero on
      any given quote, and keeping both is what lets two quotes with different licence models
      be subtracted from each other (ch22).
    formula: cores * licence_per_core + hosts * licence_per_host

  support_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: 1/year
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.07, likely: 0.11, maximum: 0.18}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "annual support as a fraction of capital cost. Triangular because it is
        negotiated inside a band the market sets rather than drawn from one: the spread is
        what different buyers get, not what varies from year to year"

  annual_support:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: capex * support_rate

  staff_fte:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: engineers, full-time equivalent
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.5, likely: 1.0, maximum: 2.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "engineers this fleet occupies, full-time equivalent. Triangular, and the shape
        cannot express what actually happens: people are not divisible, so the real
        distribution is lumpy in the way ch08 calls a regime change"

  fully_loaded_salary:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/year
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 115000, p90: 195000}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "salary, employer costs, tooling and overhead. Lognormal because pay is
        right-skewed and cannot go negative; the p90 is a senior engineer in an expensive city"

  annual_staff_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: staff_fte * fully_loaded_salary

  annual_opex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: annual_energy_cost + annual_licences + annual_support + annual_staff_cost

  lifecycle_opex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: annual_opex * horizon

  migration_cost:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: USD
    value: 0
    label: one-off cost of moving to this design
    note: >-
      A declared zero. This is the design the plan was built on, so there is nothing to move.
      A design that would replace it carries the cost of the move here: the months of running
      both, the data copied twice, the people doing that instead of their jobs. It is the line
      an incumbent's comparison never shows and a challenger's never includes, which is why it
      is a node with a source rather than a footnote (ch22).
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "nothing to migrate: the platform the plan already runs on, on the hosts already
        quoted. A challenger's scenario overrides this with the team's own estimate of the move,
        marked as what it is"
    range: [0, 1000000]

  tco:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: five-year total cost of ownership
    note: >-
      Capital, running cost over the horizon, and whatever it costs to get there. The last term
      is zero for the design the plan was built on and is the first thing to look for in a
      comparison that was not (ch22). One purchase: the horizon is the refresh cycle, so the
      refresh that ends it belongs to the next plan's capital, not this total (ch15).
    formula: capex + lifecycle_opex + migration_cost

  # -- unit economics: two denominators for one fleet ------------------------------------------

  seconds_per_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: second/year
    value: 31557600
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: "by definition, 365.25 x 86,400"

  average_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: mean request rate over the horizon
    note: >-
      The mean of the day-one and horizon means: a straight line drawn under a curve that is not
      straight, which understates the area. Stated rather than hidden, because a unit cost is
      only as defensible as its denominator (ch17).
    formula: (peak_request_rate_t0 / peak_to_mean + mean_request_rate) / 2

  requests_over_horizon:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    formula: average_request_rate * seconds_per_year * horizon

  cost_per_million_requests:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/megarequest
    label: cost per million requests
    note: >-
      The formula divides dollars by requests and the node is declared per million of them, so
      the build supplies the factor. Two honest unit costs come out of this fleet, and they tell
      different stories about the same money (ch17).
    formula: tco / requests_over_horizon

  average_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    note: "the mean of the day-one and horizon holdings, with the same understatement as above"
    formula: (stored_data_t0 + stored_data) / 2

  cost_per_stored_tb_month:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/TB/month
    label: cost per stored TB per month
    note: >-
      Divides by a horizon in years and is declared in months. Identical dimensions, a factor of
      twelve apart; a check that compared only dimensions would publish a figure twelve times too
      large and pass. sizing/units.py converts.
    formula: tco / average_stored / horizon

outputs:
  # The sizing and the price, first: what a reader of ch12 and ch18 wants.
  - hosts_recommended
  - hosts
  - tco
  - cost_per_million_requests
  - cost_per_stored_tb_month
  - capex
  - annual_opex
  - annual_energy
  # The ceilings, and what each one is about.
  - queueing_headroom
  - failure_headroom
  - cache_fill
  - disk_fill
  - scaling_loss
  - coordination_headroom
  # Part II's own figures. Terminal in the finished model, and outputs because a quantity the
  # book quotes has to be one -- a node that feeds nothing and is reported nowhere is a leftover.
  - utilisation
  - residence_time
  - waiting_time
  - concurrency
  - in_flight_unqueued
  - optimism
  - headroom_to_peak

correlations:
  - a: peak_request_rate_t0
    b: service_demand
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      The unhappy one. A busier service is usually a slower one per request — caches miss more,
      locks are held longer, the garbage collector runs while somebody is waiting. Treating the
      two as independent understates the tail of every figure in this model, and it understates
      it exactly when the fleet is busiest.

  - a: host_price
    b: network_price_per_host
    rho: 0.5
    because: >-
      Both are quoted by the same supply chain in the same quarter. A year when hosts are scarce
      is usually a year when optics are, and treating them as independent narrows the interval
      on capital cost by pretending one can save you from the other.
files.scenarios/challenger.yaml:
scenario: challenger
title: The challenger's quote, held exactly
because: >-
  A second quote for the same workload: denser hosts at a higher price each, drawing more power
  each, licensed per host rather than per core, with a higher support rate, and a one-off cost
  of moving that the incumbent does not pay. Every line is pinned, because a quote is a number.
  The host count is what the model's own sizing rule recommends at the point estimate for this
  host, so both designs are sized to the same margins by the same rule; the licence per core is
  a declared zero because this quote has no such line; and the move is the team's estimate, not
  the vendor's. Same seed and the same pinned inputs as the incumbent, so that the two totals
  can be subtracted future by future (ch22).
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  cores_per_host: 64
  ram_per_host: 256
  disk_per_host: 8
  host_price: 26000
  host_power: 700
  licence_per_core: 0
  licence_per_host: 2600
  support_rate: 0.13
  hosts: 14
  migration_cost: 250000
files.scenarios/incumbent.yaml:
scenario: incumbent
title: The incumbent's quote, held exactly
because: >-
  The design the plan was built on, priced as a quote rather than as a band. Every line a vendor
  would put on a quote is pinned at the value the model's point estimate already uses, so this
  scenario's point figures are the reference scenario's, and its interval is only what a quote
  does not fix: the workload, the growth, the electricity, the people. It is one side of ch22's
  comparison, and it pins the same inputs as the challenger so that the two totals can be
  subtracted future by future.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  cores_per_host: 16
  ram_per_host: 64
  disk_per_host: 2
  host_price: 6538.348415311009
  host_power: 310.45548849896676
  licence_per_core: 79.99999999999997
  licence_per_host: 0
  support_rate: 0.11795163177004572
  hosts: 54
  migration_cost: 0
files.scenarios/power_first.yaml:
scenario: power_first
title: Sized from the power budget inwards
because: >-
  A rack has a power budget before it has a capital budget, and where that is the binding
  constraint the sizing runs the other way: watts available, divided by watts per host, gives a
  host count, and everything else follows from it. Here the fleet is held to what a
  sixteen-kilowatt allocation supports at the reference PUE, which is fewer hosts than any of
  the three chains asked for - and ch16 is about reading the ceilings that result rather than
  arguing with the electricity supply.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  hosts: 36
files.scenarios/reference.yaml:
scenario: reference
title: Reference scenario
because: >-
  The scenario every figure in the book quotes unless it says otherwise. Nothing is overridden:
  this is the model as declared, so that a figure and the model file cannot drift apart.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides: {}
files.scenarios/sized_for_growth.yaml:
scenario: sized_for_growth
title: Sized for the growth we might get, not the growth we expect
because: >-
  The reference scenario buys what the point estimates recommend, and the model then puts a
  good share of its futures over the knee and past the working set's margin. This scenario buys
  the fleet the p90 growth case needs instead, and is here so the two can be read side by side:
  what the extra capital buys is a number, the fall in every P(over) is a number, and the
  decision between them is a judgement somebody has to make and defend (ch21).
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  hosts: 131
files.scenarios/twice_the_hosts.yaml:
scenario: twice_the_hosts
title: Twice the hosts
because: >-
  The same workload on twice the fleet. Here so that ch06 and ch07 can be read against each
  other: doubling the hosts halves the utilisation and does far less than halve the residence
  time, and it does not double the throughput either.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  hosts: 108

title: A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts

files.model.yaml:
model: observability
title: An observability platform — metrics, logs and traces
currency: USD

description: >-
  The book's second model, and the counterweight to the web service. Three multiplicative
  chains hang off the same few roots, so they are correlated whether or not anybody says so; label
  cardinality is a product of uncertain counts and therefore dominates everything downstream of
  it; the control knobs are sampling and retention rather than money; and there are three separate
  outputs with three separate ceilings, which no single number can summarise.

  It also has a hole in it. Spans per request is a property of somebody's instrumented
  application, not of any corpus or any machine, so this repository cannot measure it — and the
  whole traces chain is therefore shown as unmeasured rather than filled in with a plausible
  number. That is not a gap waiting to be tidied up. It is what an honest sizing model looks like
  before the measurement is taken, and it is on a published page for exactly that reason.

nodes:

  # -- shared roots ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Everything below flows from these five. That is what makes the three chains correlated by
  # construction: they are not three models, they are one estate seen three ways.

  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: host
    value: 1200
    note: >-
      No band: an estate is a thing you can count, and this one has been counted. What it does
      next is growth_factor's business, not this node's.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "stated estate size (ch02)"}
    range: [50, 3000]

  request_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 8000.0, likely: 25000.0, maximum: 90000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch03 — the busy hour across the estate, not the daily mean. Triangular: a
        minimum, a likely and a maximum is the whole of what a dashboard gives you, and the
        maximum is the busiest hour anybody has looked at rather than the busiest one there
        will be"
    range: [2000, 200000]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.15, p90: 1.70}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — telemetry grows faster than the traffic it describes, because teams add
        instrumentation as well as load. Lognormal like any growth rate — it compounds and
        cannot go negative — and wider than the web service's for the same reason its
        median is higher"

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 3
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the planning horizon for this platform"}
    range: [1, 5]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    note: "as in the web service model: an exponent has to be a pure number"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  growth_factor:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  # -- label cardinality: the combinatorial node ------------------------------------------------

  label_values_endpoint:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 6.0, maximum: 20.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "distinct routes appearing as a label value. Triangular because somebody could
        go and count them this afternoon; the maximum is the routes that exist today, and a
        new service adds to it"

  label_values_status:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 3.0, maximum: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "distinct status classes kept as a label. Triangular, and the one input in this
        model whose bounds are genuinely hard: a request cannot carry a status the code does
        not emit"

  label_values_accidental:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: accidental label values
    note: >-
      The label nobody planned. A pod name under a rolling deploy, a customer id added during an
      incident, a version string. Lognormal and wide, because the failure mode is multiplicative:
      whatever it is, it multiplies every series that carries it, and the distribution has to be
      able to express "usually nothing, occasionally catastrophic".
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.0, p90: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — the cardinality explosion, as a distribution rather than as a warning.
        Lognormal because this one has no ceiling: a label carrying a user id multiplies the
        series count by a number nobody chose, and a triangular would assert a maximum that
        does not exist"

  label_cardinality:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: label cardinality
    note: >-
      A product of uncertain counts, which is why it is lognormal-ish whether or not anybody chose
      that, and why it dominates the tornado for every metrics figure in this model. Multiplying
      three quantities that are each uncertain by a factor of three gives one uncertain by a
      factor of twenty-seven, and no amount of care about the other inputs recovers that.
    formula: label_values_endpoint * label_values_status * label_values_accidental

  # -- chain one: metrics ------------------------------------------------------------------------

  base_metrics_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/host
    value: 60
    label: metric names per host
    note: >-
      No band: scrape one host and list them. The uncertainty in this chain is what the labels
      multiply that list by, and label_cardinality carries it.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "distinct metric names exposed per host, before labels"}
    range: [10, 400]

  active_series:
    kind: derived
    unit: series
    formula: hosts * base_metrics_per_host * label_cardinality * growth_factor

  scrape_interval:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: second
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12): doubling it halves the metrics
      chain and loses resolution that cannot be recovered afterwards"}
    range: [10, 120]

  one_sample_per_series:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: sample/series
    value: 1
    note: "one scrape takes one sample from one series. A rate is a count over a duration, and the
      count needs a unit before the division means anything"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  sample_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: sample/series/second
    formula: one_sample_per_series / scrape_interval

  metrics_sample_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/sample
    label: bytes per sample, compressed
    result: metrics-sample-bytes

  metrics_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: metrics ingest
    formula: active_series * sample_rate * metrics_sample_bytes

  metrics_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 400
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [15, 800]

  metrics_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: metrics_ingest * metrics_retention

  # -- chain two: logs ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  lines_per_request:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: line/request
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3.0, likely: 9.0, maximum: 30.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "application log lines emitted per request served. Triangular, from reading a
        sample of the logs — and the maximum is the part to distrust, because a debug flag
        left on in production is outside it"

  log_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 1.0
    label: fraction of log lines kept
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12): drop and aggregation rules"}
    range: [0.05, 1.0]

  log_line_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: line/second
    formula: request_rate * lines_per_request * log_keep_rate * growth_factor

  logs_line_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/line
    label: bytes per log line, compressed
    result: logs-line-bytes

  logs_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: logs ingest
    formula: log_line_rate * logs_line_bytes

  logs_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [3, 365]

  logs_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: logs_ingest * logs_retention

  # -- chain three: traces, and the constant nobody has measured ------------------------------------

  spans_per_request:
    kind: measured
    unit: span/request
    label: spans per request
    note: >-
      Not measurable from anything in this repository. It is a property of one instrumented
      application at one version, so it belongs to the `estate` target — an observation somebody
      takes of a system they run, disclosed rather than verified (ch03). Until somebody takes it,
      every figure below is absent rather than estimated.
    result: traces-spans-per-request

  trace_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.05
    label: trace sampling rate
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12), and the one with the widest
      range: head sampling at 1% and at 100% are two different platforms"}
    range: [0.001, 1.0]

  span_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: span/second
    formula: request_rate * spans_per_request * trace_keep_rate * growth_factor

  traces_span_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/span
    label: bytes per span, compressed
    result: traces-span-bytes

  traces_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: traces ingest
    formula: span_rate * traces_span_bytes

  traces_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 14
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [1, 90]

  traces_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: traces_ingest * traces_retention

  # -- output one: the ingest pipeline ---------------------------------------------------------------

  known_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: ingest, metrics and logs only
    note: >-
      Metrics plus logs, and deliberately *not* the total. It is a lower bound with a whole chain
      missing from it, and ch19 is about exactly this shape of error: a number that is correct
      arithmetic over an incomplete structure looks identical to a number that is right.
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest

  total_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest + traces_ingest

  collector_cores:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core
    value: 16
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the ingest tier"}
    range: [8, 512]

  collector_throughput_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: MB/s/core
    value: 6
    note: >-
      No band, and giving a quote one would be inventing a range nobody quoted. A vendor states a
      single number; the spread belongs to the measurement, and collector_throughput_measured
      below carries it with a standard error.
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "throughput per core as documented by the collector. Unverified here, and marked as
        a claim in every figure it appears in"

  collector_throughput_measured:
    kind: measured
    unit: MB/s/core
    label: collector throughput per core, measured
    note: >-
      The same quantity as the node above, taken rather than quoted. It needs the reference
      machine (`rig`) and nobody has run it, so the ceiling built on it is absent while the
      ceiling built on the vendor's claim is not. Reading those two rows next to each other is
      most of ch03.
    result: collector-throughput-per-core

  quoted_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_quoted

  measured_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_measured

  quoted_pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, quoted
    of: known_ingest / quoted_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      A queueing ceiling, not a capacity one (ch06), so the margin is large: a pipeline at 80% of
      quoted throughput has a queue in front of it, and a queue in front of an ingest pipeline is
      dropped telemetry exactly when something is going wrong. Understated twice over — the
      numerator excludes traces and the denominator is a vendor's claim.

  pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, measured
    of: total_ingest / measured_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      The honest version of the row above, and it cannot be computed. Both halves are missing a
      measurement, which is the correct output of this model today.

  # -- output two: the retention store -----------------------------------------------------------

  usable_tb_per_node:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/node
    value: 40
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "usable capacity per storage node after replication"}
    range: [20, 400]

  store_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 12
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the retention tier"}
    range: [5, 400]

  installed_usable:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: store_nodes * usable_tb_per_node

  known_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: stored, metrics and logs only
    formula: metrics_stored + logs_stored

  store_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: retention store fill
    of: known_stored / installed_usable
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.3
    because: >-
      Capacity, with a rebuild reserve (ch11) — and again a lower bound, because the traces chain
      is not in the numerator. A verdict of `ok` here means "ok, ignoring traces", which is a
      different claim and one the reader should be made to notice.

  # -- output three: the query path -----------------------------------------------------------------

  queries_per_second:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: query/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 12.0, maximum: 60.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "dashboards, alert rules and people, at the busy hour. Triangular because two of
        those three are countable and the third is not"

  series_per_query_base:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/query
    label: series per query, before labels
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 40.0, likely: 300.0, maximum: 2000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "how many distinct metric-name-and-host combinations one dashboard panel or alert
        rule covers, before any label expansion. Triangular, and wide: dashboards differ from
        each other more than anything else in this model does"

  series_per_query:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/query
    note: >-
      The same cardinality node that drives the metrics ingest chain drives this one too, by a
      different route: a label that multiplies the series a scrape produces also multiplies the
      series a query has to walk past to ignore. That is why one accidental label breaks two
      ceilings at once, and why turning down scrape interval and retention — which fix the first
      — does nothing at all for the second (ch12).
    formula: series_per_query_base * label_cardinality

  query_series_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: queries_per_second * series_per_query

  query_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 24
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the query tier"}
    range: [2, 120]

  query_scan_rate_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/second/node
    value: 90000
    note: >-
      No band, for the same reason as the collector's quoted throughput: a quote is one number,
      and widening it here would put a range in the vendor's mouth. Nobody has measured this one,
      so nothing in this model disputes it yet.
    provenance: {kind: vendor_claim, source: "series scanned per second per query node, quoted"}

  query_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: query_nodes * query_scan_rate_quoted

  query_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: query path utilisation
    of: query_series_rate / query_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      Queueing again, and the tier where a breach is most visible: a dashboard that times out
      during an incident is the failure people remember. Cardinality feeds this and the ingest
      ceiling by different routes, so a single accidental label breaks both at once.

  # -- a small cost tail ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  storage_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/TB/month
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 9.0, p90: 24.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "all-in cost of a usable TB-month on this tier. Lognormal because it is a price —
        and carried across by hand from whichever storage tier's unit economics somebody had to
        hand, rather than by sampling, which is the seam ch18 is about"

  known_storage_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/month
    label: retention cost, metrics and logs only
    formula: known_stored * storage_price

outputs:
  - metrics_ingest
  - logs_ingest
  - traces_ingest
  - traces_stored
  - known_ingest
  - known_stored
  - active_series
  - label_cardinality
  - known_storage_cost
  - store_fill
  - quoted_pipeline_utilisation
  - query_utilisation
  - pipeline_utilisation

correlations:
  - a: annual_growth
    b: label_values_accidental
    rho: 0.5
    because: >-
      A platform that is growing is a platform that is being changed, and labels arrive with
      changes. Treating the two as independent makes the metrics interval narrower than the
      estate warrants — ch14 measures by how much.

  - a: request_rate
    b: lines_per_request
    rho: 0.3
    because: >-
      Weak and positive: busier services tend to be the chattier ones. Small enough to be worth
      including as an example of a correlation that barely matters, which is a useful thing for a
      reader to see beside one that does.

  - a: request_rate
    b: queries_per_second
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      A busier platform is one more people are watching. Moderate rather than strong: most query
      load comes from alert rules and dashboards on timers, which do not care how busy anything
      is — right up until an incident, when they all fire at once and nobody is looking at the
      model.
files.scenarios/knobs_turned_down.yaml:
scenario: knobs_turned_down
title: The four knobs, turned down
because: >-
  The same estate with every control knob moved: 60-second scrapes, 90-day metric retention, a
  tenth of the log lines kept, and 1% trace sampling. Here so that ch12 can put a number on what
  each knob buys — and so the reader can see that the knobs do not touch cardinality at all,
  which is the input that dominates everything.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  scrape_interval: 60
  metrics_retention: 90
  log_keep_rate: 0.1
  trace_keep_rate: 0.01
files.scenarios/reference.yaml:
scenario: reference
title: Reference scenario
because: >-
  The platform as declared: 30-second scrapes, 400-day metric retention, 30-day logs, 5% trace
  sampling. Every figure the book quotes for this model comes from here unless it says otherwise.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides: {}

title: An observability platform — metrics, logs and traces
